A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Trust-Region Search (TRS) work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–J support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material and renumbered sample galleries.

before.justification: v1 reports original text-to-image, molecule-generation, and protein-design experiments in Section 4, plus ablations and sampling analyses in Appendices D–E.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, adaptation ablations, and a qualitative comparison with FLUX.1-dev.

M1.justification: The proposed TRS procedure remains unchanged: warm-up, masked Sobol/Gaussian perturbations, adaptive region lengths, global top-k recentering, and appendix restart rules. The fixed-radius variant is an experimental ablation, not a replacement of the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions use DrawBench image generation, QM9 molecule property matching, and protein design with 50 or 100 residues. Existing ODE/SDE scenarios are retained. The new FLUX.1-dev comparison uses DrawBench prompts and changes the model configuration rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds evaluated FK-Steering, DAS, and diagonal CMA-ES baselines. CMA-ES also enters the molecule and protein comparisons in Figures 7–8. Fixed-radius TRS becomes an ablation comparator, and new Figure 15 compares optimized SD1.5 with vanilla SD1.5 and FLUX.1-dev. The original evaluated baselines remain.

E3.justification: Table 4 substantially revises reported OC-Flow settings: image step size changes from 0.25 to 2.5, optimization steps from 50 to 15 for images and 50 to 5 for molecules, and the molecule weight constraint from 0.4 to 0.01; weight decay also changes. Its scores remain unchanged, so rerunning is not established. New protocols include the fixed-radius control and Figure 15's 1,500-reward-evaluation comparison.

E4.justification: v2 directly tests removal of trust-region adaptation across all three modalities in Table 3 and Figures 7–8; the image comparison explicitly retains warm-up and top-k selection. This isolates a central component beyond v1's existing parameter and recentering studies. Appendix J also adds a qualitative case study of source-noise optimization versus choosing a larger backbone. Existing Appendix D–E analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The mean-best reporting practice is retained. v2 adds no repeated-run or seed protocol, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for either retained or newly added comparisons.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial baseline and ablation results while retaining the original main alignment scores. Table 3's new CMA-ES results change the SDXL-Lightning ranking: ImageReward is 1.67 versus TRS's 1.66, and HPSv2 is 0.344 versus 0.340. New resource entries and FLUX examples are reported. Figure 13 also changes DTS's SD1.5/HPS memory bar from approximately 9.65 to 11.9 GB.

T1.justification: The TRS objective, proposal equations, and adaptation mathematics are unchanged; no theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is added. Appendix F.3's standard CMA-ES sampling formula documents a baseline. Appendix G.2 repairs malformed inequality symbols rather than establishing a new theoretical result.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about black-box source-noise alignment, performance across three modalities, and minimal tuning. These core assertions are not recalibrated despite the expanded comparisons.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the fixed-radius comparison as evidence for adaptation, attributes CMA-ES's molecule performance tentatively to tuning sensitivity, and presents source-noise search as an alternative to increasing backbone size. It also expands discussion of SMC reward costs and solver applicability. The existing reward-model and diversity limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Table 4 and Appendix F.3 add CMA-ES implementation details, including diagonal covariance, zero initialization, initial step size 0.2, population sizes, and normalization. Table 4 revises OC-Flow settings and removes Fast Direct settings from molecule/protein columns where it was not evaluated. Appendix G.2 makes the designability inequalities readable. Code and model-access information is otherwise retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Hansen and Ostermeier (2001) for CMA-ES and explains its relationship to the already cited evolutionary-search work of Jajal et al. Previously cited SMC approaches are explicitly named FK-Steering and DAS and discussed further. The broader positioning of TRS as TuRBO-inspired black-box source-noise search remains.

P1.justification: Changes include localized explanatory additions, grammar corrections, clearer appendix references, expanded affiliations, an acceptance notice, and contribution and acknowledgment statements. The main narrative and section organization remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: Table 3 gains comparison rows and memory/runtime columns; Table 4 and Figures 7–8 expand. v2 adds Figure 15, reformats Algorithm 1 across the page width, revises captions, and corrects Figure 13's GNSO legend to FD. Existing sample galleries are retained as Figures 16–19. These are targeted changes within the same overall layout.

improvement.justification: The added CMA-ES/SMC comparisons and direct adaptation ablation make the empirical evidence more informative, while implementation details improve reproducibility. The benefit is limited by unresolved inconsistencies: Section 4.1 still claims universal TRS superiority although CMA-ES wins both SDXL-Lightning rewards, and substantial OC-Flow setting revisions are not reconciled with unchanged scores. Overall, v2 provides better comparative evidence, but its interpretation and protocol transparency do not improve commensurately.
